title: The Harbor, part one
summary: I tell you what I am not, who this path is for and how it works, then hand you the first idea everything else hangs on, which is that your AI is the teammate who never asks questions. It is my journey and an invitation, not a tutorial.

stops.title: Before you set off

beats.text: Hi, I'm Tjakoen. Let me start with what I'm not. I'm not an expert. Six months of using this every day is my whole credential. So take everything here as one person's notes, not as rules.

beats.quote: This isn't a tutorial or a step-by-step guide.
beats.text: And this isn't a tutorial. It's my journey so far, and what I picked up on the way. If you disagree with me, good. Tell me what you did instead.
I mention the two days because it's the point, not a flex. If I can go from an idea to a working thing that fast, so can you.

In case we haven't met. I manage engineers at Career Team, and I teach software engineering part-time at a university. Nine years in. Mostly that means reading other people's code and finding the problems politely. The AI part is the last six months. If you'd rather check who's talking before you trust them, my About page has the rest. I'd encourage that.

**Beat X**
highlight: why-i-started-over | figure: learning path as a line of six places

Here's the shape of the whole path. The Harbor comes first, and it's the short on-ramp: the basics in plain words, plus Claude Academy outside this site. Then the mainland, in order of difficulty, ending at the deep technical notes. You don't have to walk all of it. The order is on purpose, so you meet the ideas before the deeper notes lean on them.

beats.quote: AI is a reason to learn them harder
beats.text: You'll hear me assume you can code a little. That's on purpose. The AI doesn't replace that skill, it raises the stakes on it, because you're the one who has to notice when it's wrong.

beats.quote: You can hand the bricklaying to an AI.
beats.text: Here's the idea I keep coming back to. Architect and bricklayer. The AI lays bricks, fast. You decide what the building is. And there's a second line I care about. Plenty of people ship what they don't understand and can't fix. That's blind vibe coding. I'm after the orchestrator, who can explain and repair what gets built.

runes.quote: You can hand the bricklaying to an AI.

stops.trial: Write one sentence on whether you see yourself as a builder or a coder right now, and why. Or write down what you hope to get out of this path.
digest: I am six months in and not an expert, and this is a journey, not a tutorial.
This path assumes you can program a little. It does not teach that.
You can hand the bricklaying to the AI, but not the drawing. Aim to be the orchestrator, not the blind vibe coder.

stops.title: How the path works

beats.text: Every stop ends with a small thing to try, your turn. Do it, or do something different. Either way, that's where it sticks.
Nothing here checks your work. I think that's the honest way to do it. It also means the only person you can fool is you.

One thing before you cross. The free lessons at Claude Academy, academy dot claude dot com, give you the basics. Do those first. After that, what I show works with any harness. And if your setup misbehaves, you don't need to know why before you ask the AI to help you fix it. It sounds circular. It works.

There's a project running through the Harbor. Your portfolio. Got one, add to it. Don't, I'll give you a small starting skeleton on GitHub Pages. Its centerpiece is an AI roadmap page, one entry per lesson, in your own words. It's also a home for your certificates and badges, including your Claude Academy ones. The design and the words are yours. Make it a timeline, a zine, a game. And because it's public, keep your keys and personal details out of it.

beats.quote: copy what's useful, change the rest
beats.text: This is your permission slip. I tried every organizing app there is, and each one wanted me to adapt to its system. I couldn't, so I built one that adapted to me. My team did the same thing, and no two of their setups match. Take what's useful, change the rest, and show me what you made.

runes.quote: copy what's useful, change the rest

stops.trial: Do the Claude Academy basics if you have not, then decide whether to add to a portfolio you have or start from the skeleton.
digest: Start at the Harbor, then cross to the mainland. You build your own portfolio along the way.
Progress is self-reported, so the only person you can fool is you.
What I do works for me. Copy what is useful, change the rest, and show me what you make.

stops.title: The teammate who never asks questions

beats.text: Picture the group project teammate who says "got it" and asks nothing. They aren't lazy. They guessed so they wouldn't look lost. That's your AI.

Here's the honest reason I do any of this. I'm terrible at multitasking, and I strive to be lazy. A lazy programmer is an effective one, because they put their effort into making life easier. But lazy doesn't mean skipping the careful part. It means doing it once, up front. I built the rails before I opened the throttle.

beats.quote: Each of those was a choice
beats.text:
Ask for "a portfolio site" and count what comes back. A hero banner, a color scheme, a bio in a stranger's voice, projects you never built. Choices you never made, delivered in a confident voice. That confidence is the risk.

**Beat X**
highlight: it-says-yes-to-everything | figure: two paths from the same request

Look at the two paths side by side. The same request goes in on both. On the left, nobody says where the gaps are, so the agent guesses, and you find the wrong result late. On the right, a short brief goes first, and what comes back is something you can check against what you wrote. The only thing that changed is what you handed over before it started.

Working with AI is a lot like mentoring, and I found I already knew how. It's a capable junior, or a student rushing through an activity to finish. Fast and willing, and it knows only what you told it.

beats.quote: the scarce thing stops being code and becomes intent
beats.text: And here's why it matters. When the AI types, the scarce thing is no longer code. It's intent. In my own repos, the documentation is the work and the code is the cheap part.

runes.quote: Each of those was a choice
the scarce thing stops being code and becomes intent

stops.trial: Ask your AI for something vague, like a portfolio site, and list every choice it made that you did not.
digest: An AI agent behaves like the group project teammate who says got it and asks nothing.
It fills every gap with a guess, and then sounds sure.
It cannot think for you, so you keep the intent. Being lazy on purpose means doing the careful part once, up front.

stops.title: Brief it, and stay the orchestrator

beats.text:
Before I ask for anything, three lines: the goal, what done looks like, what to leave alone. The middle one is where people get stuck. If I can't say what done looks like, I've found something I haven't decided yet. Better to find that now.

**Beat X**
highlight: say-what-done-looks-like | figure: the brief has three parts

Here are the three lines side by side. Nothing in them is code. The middle one is shaded because it's the one people get stuck on, and it tells you whether the task is ready to hand over at all. A first-year with a clear brief will often get a better result than an expert with a vague one.

There was a week I looked at what had shipped across my repos and couldn't explain half of it. All worked, tests green. Output going up while understanding stays flat is debt with a nice green dashboard on top. That's the week I stopped, and it's why I ask one question about anything the AI builds: could I explain this, and fix it if the AI weren't here tomorrow?
The AI doesn't. Close the session and it starts blank. So the brief goes in a file, where it can read it every time. Writing it down isn't paperwork. It's how you give a forgetful teammate a memory.

Your turn. Brief your portfolio, or ask for it with no brief and list the guesses, or brief something else. Then compare what you get with what you wrote. The gap shows you what you hadn't decided yet. I might be overselling the brief, so try both and see which fits you.

runes.quote: could I explain this, and could I fix it if the AI weren't here

stops.trial: Write the three-part brief for your portfolio, or its roadmap section, give it to your AI, and compare what you get with what you wrote.
digest: A brief has three parts. The goal, what done looks like, and what not to touch.
If you cannot explain it and fix it without the AI, you adopted it. You did not build it.
The AI forgets between sessions, so the brief has to live in a file.
